query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Promoting dynamic grain refinement in a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating—so that during high‐temperature sliding an ultra‐nanocrystalline, partially amorphous surface layer forms—will reduce wear and smooth out the microscopic deformation (i.e. reduce abrupt slip events) relative to the as-deposited condition.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a baseline, conventional grain size distribution and microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment or sliding protocol designed to enhance dynamic grain refinement during sliding (e.g., by pre-conditioning at elevated temperature or controlled strain rate) that promotes the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., temperatures above ~600°C) under controlled load such that dynamic microstructural evolution (grain refinement and partial amorphization) can occur.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer via dynamic amorphization during sliding.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature sliding, controlled processing promotes rapid formation of a refined microstructure. This significantly increases the grain boundary area which impedes dislocation motion and distributes stress more evenly. The result is more uniform plastic deformation (fewer sudden slips) and lower abrasive wear compared to coatings with a coarser microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline coating, the dynamically refined coating will exhibit lower wear rates and smoother (less serrated) microscopic deformation behavior during sliding tests in high-temperature regimes.
generation.baseline: The FeNiCrCoCu coating in its as-deposited state without any additional treatment to promote grain refinement.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions where dynamic microstructural transformation is possible; it may not apply at lower temperatures or in non-sliding contact where thermal activation is insufficient.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between the degree of grain refinement and the magnitude of wear rate reduction is uncertain. Additionally, high-temperature oxidation or other environmental interactions may also influence wear behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings: one set kept in the as-deposited state as a baseline and another subjected to a controlled heat treatment or pre-sliding protocol designed to enhance dynamic grain refinement. Then, perform identical high-temperature sliding wear tests on both sets and characterize the near-surface microstructures (using, e.g., TEM/SEM).
measurements: Wear volume loss or wear rate under a standardized load during sliding.
Microstructural analysis (grain size, presence of amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline layer) of the worn surfaces.
Analysis of the stress-strain response during sliding to monitor deformation serrations.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in wear resistance (lower wear rate) and do not exhibit the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous near-surface layer compared to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
